title: Yahya
def: John the Baptist, the son of Zechariah, whom the Quran praises as a prophet, noble and chaste.
what: Zechariah prayed for an heir, and the angels gave him good news of “a son whose name is Yahya; We have not given that name to anyone before” (19:7). “O Yahya, hold the Book with strength.” We gave him judgement as a child, tenderness from Us and purity, and he was devout, dutiful to his parents, and not arrogant or disobedient (19:12–14). He confirms “a word from God” (3:39), meaning Jesus.

title: Ya Arham al-Rahimin
def: O Most Merciful of those who show mercy; said in any need of help
what: This is an invocation of Allah, meaning “O Most Merciful of those who show mercy”. Muslims say it when they need help, in illness, distress, fear or ordinary requests. The phrase comes from the Quran, where Moses prays “You are the Most Merciful of the merciful” (7:151) and Job calls on his Lord with the same words (21:83). The superlative places Allah’s mercy above that of every human being. People say the phrase aloud or silently, singly or as part of a longer supplication, and it often accompanies other names of Allah. It is a form of duʿāʾ, an address to Allah, and needs no special occasion or place.
misread: That it can be reduced to “O Merciful”, which loses the superlative above all who show mercy.

title: Yaqin
def: Certainty about the truth of Islam and its claims, needing no further proof
what: Yaqīn is certainty, a settled conviction that leaves no room for doubt. In Ismail al Faruqi’s account it is certainty about the truth of Islam and its claims, which requires no further proof. The Quran commands the Prophet to worship his Lord until certainty comes to him (15:99), and commentators generally take this to mean death. The Quran names three levels of certainty: ʿilm al-yaqīn (102:5), ʿayn al-yaqīn (102:7) and ḥaqq al-yaqīn (69:51). Scholars, especially the Sufis, have used them to describe growth from knowledge to sight to direct experience. The opposite of yaqīn is doubt, ẓann or shakk.
misread: That it is blind belief, when the sources join certainty to knowledge and reflection.

title: Yusr
def: That which is possible without hardship; ease
what: Yusr means ease: what a person can do without hardship. The Quran says “Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship” (2:185) and “with hardship comes ease” (94:5-6). Another verse promises that Allah will bring ease after hardship (65:7). The principle shapes the law. Jurists hold that hardship calls for relief, and the sharia allows concessions: the traveller may shorten the prayer, and the sick and the traveller may postpone the fast. A saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in Sahih al-Bukhari states that the religion is ease. The word ʿusr, hardship, is its opposite.
misread: That ease means laxity, when it is a stated principle of the law with defined concessions.
